[PEP 779](https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/), [What's New 3.14](https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html), [3.14 howto](https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html)
- **The ecosystem has dropped 3.13t.** manylinux removed its 3.13t images on 2026-05-07. cibuildwheel deprecated 3.13t, and Pillow and PyTorch stopped publishing 3.13t wheels. [PyTorch](https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386), [cibuildwheel](https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/pull/2787), [Pillow](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/latest/releasenotes/12.3.0.html)

**Your dependencies on 3.13t**
- **NumPy:** 2.4.0 still had cp313t wheels, but the current 2.5.4 has none. 2.5 also adds free-threaded ufunc scaling fixes. [2.4.0](https://pypi.org/project/numpy/2.4.0/), [2.5.4](https://pypi.org/project/numpy/), [2.5 notes](https://numpy.org/doc/2.5/release/2.5.0-notes.html)
- **pydantic:** free-threading support was added as experimental in 2.11. Race-condition fixes for the free-threaded build kept landing as late as 2.14 (Sep 2026). pydantic-core has had no cp313t wheels since at least 2.41.5 (Nov 2025). [2.11 blog](https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-11-release), [changelog](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/changelog/), [2.41.5](https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/2.41.5/)
- **lxml:** stable 6.x builds on 3.13t but switches the GIL back on when imported. Forcing the GIL off and calling lxml from several threads will likely crash it. Real support starts in 7.0, which is still alpha and only targets 3.14t and later. [LP#2111289](https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289), [LP#2069434](https://bugs.launchpad.net/bugs/2069434), [changes](https://lxml.de/7.0/changes-7.0.0a3.html), [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/lxml/)

1. **Ask the platform team for a 3.14t runtime.** Current NumPy and pydantic both ship cp314t manylinux x86-64 wheels.
2. **Treat lxml as the blocker.** Either wait for lxml 7.0 final or test the alpha in staging. If you can't wait, move XML parsing into a separate worker process, or run it in a single thread behind a lock. A lock is the riskier option.
3. **Fail fast at startup.** After all imports, assert `not sys._is_gil_enabled()`. A dependency can quietly turn the GIL back on and undo the speedup. [guide](https://py-free-threading.github.io/running-gil-disabled/)
4. **Audit shared state.** Don't share mutable NumPy arrays between threads, and avoid object arrays. [NumPy](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/thread_safety.html), [guide](https://py-free-threading.github.io/)
5. **Benchmark before switching.** Compare 3.14t threads against your current setup (multiprocessing, or NumPy operations that release the GIL). Until 3.14t is available, stay on 3.13 with processes.

I read about 30 sources in total; the ones listed here are those the conclusions rest on.

# Is free-threaded 3.13t production-ready for your service?

**No.** The best path to no-GIL is 3.14t, which means asking for an exception to your 3.13 pin. Even on 3.14t, lxml will probably turn the GIL back on until lxml 7.0 is final.

## Why not 3.13t

- **It is officially experimental.** The CPython docs warn of bugs and about a 40% single-thread slowdown. They also list memory growth from immortal objects and crashes when iterators or frames are shared across threads. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- **3.14 is the first supported phase.** PEP 779 sets that status, with a target of at most 15% single-thread overhead. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ Official 3.14 figures put the overhead at roughly 1–10%. https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html
- **The ecosystem is dropping 3.13t.**
  - manylinux removed cp313t on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch followed. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
  - Pillow 12.3 dropped its cp313t wheels. https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/latest/releasenotes/12.3.0.html
- **Your dependencies' current releases show cp314t wheels but no cp313t ones.** The researchers saw only partial PyPI file lists, so this isn't certain. On 3.13t you would be stuck on older pins, such as pydantic-core 2.34.1, or building from source.
  - https://pypi.org/project/numpy/
  - https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/
  - https://pypi.org/project/lxml/

## The lxml blocker

Per lxml's bug tracker, its cp314t wheels re-enable the GIL on import. Forcing the GIL off was expected to crash. The fix is targeted at lxml 7.0, and only an alpha had been found. https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289

## Other caveats

- NumPy's free-threading support is still labelled experimental, and arrays are only safe to share read-only. https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/thread_safety.html
- Turning the GIL off can make code slower. One threaded benchmark took 3.61 s without the GIL versus 2.38 s with it, because of refcount contention on shared objects. https://discuss.python.org/t/slower-performance-with-disable-gil-on-threaded-nearest-neighbor-benchmark-10m-points/95365
- 3.14t still has open crash reports. https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/141965

## What to do

1. **Now:** stay on GIL 3.13 and use multiprocessing for CPU-bound work.
2. **Request a 3.14t exception** and add a separate 3.14t CI job.
3. **Check the GIL at startup.** Assert `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is `False` after all imports, because the GIL can come back silently.
4. **Wait for lxml 7.0 final**, or put a lock around lxml calls when running with `PYTHON_GIL=0`.
5. **Benchmark your real workload** at 1 thread and at N threads, against both GIL 3.14 and multiprocessing. Avoid mutating shared arrays, models or iterators in hot paths.
6. **Pilot before rolling out** generally.

**Open question:** whether lxml 7.0 final has shipped. Check its changelog before planning: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt

# Short answer: you don't need to stop because of this headline.

**Where "91%" comes from.** It comes from a 2024 conference poster, not a peer-reviewed paper. The study used US survey data (NHANES) on about 20,000 adults. Eating windows were estimated from **just two 24-hour food recalls**, and deaths were tracked for about 8 years. The AHA called it preliminary, and the authors said it doesn't show causation. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death

**Why the evidence is weak**
- **Small group.** Only about 414 people (2%) had windows under 8 hours, and about 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. That group had more smokers, higher BMI, and different demographics. Death from all causes was *not* higher. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Expert criticism.** Independent statisticians made several points. Two days of recall don't capture long-term habits. Sick people may eat less, so illness could cause the short window rather than the reverse. Shift work and poverty could explain both the eating pattern and the risk. Weight, blood pressure and lipids were missing. https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/
- **The published version (2025)** reports a hazard ratio of 2.35 (95% CI 1.39–3.98). It still finds no link with deaths from all causes, and the authors acknowledge residual confounding. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/
- **A second analysis of the same dataset** found a U-shaped curve with the lowest risk at about 11–12 hours. It shares the same flaws, so it doesn't count as independent confirmation. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12610411/
- **A UK cohort followed for 22 years** found no link between eating-window length and death. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12411609

**What trials show.** Randomized trials find that time-restricted eating gives modest weight loss, about the same as ordinary calorie restriction, with neutral to slightly favorable effects on heart risk factors. No trial has measured deaths. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12175170/

**For you specifically**
- **Your window may not even fall in the risk group.** A deliberate 16:8 window is exactly 8 hours. In these analyses that likely falls in the 8–10 h group, which showed no excess risk in people without existing heart disease. I couldn't confirm the exact cut-off.
- **A more realistic concern is muscle loss.** One 16:8 trial found loss of lean mass. Eat enough protein and do resistance training. https://www.hawaii.edu/news/2020/10/09/intermittent-fasting-study/
- **Judge it by your own results.** If 16:8 keeps your weight, blood pressure and lipids in good shape, this study gives little reason to stop. If it isn't working, regular calorie control works just as well.

**What the claim is based on**

It used US survey data (NHANES) on about 20,000 adults, and each person's eating window was judged from just **two days of recalled meals**. People who ate within less than 8 hours had a 91% higher risk of dying from heart disease than people eating over 12–16 hours. It found no rise in deaths overall. ([AHA](https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death?print=1))
- **How small:** Only 414 people, about 2% of the sample, ate within under 8 hours, and 31 of them died of heart disease. ([TCTMD](https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality))
- **Who was in that group:** It had about 60% more smokers, more people with higher weight, and far more Black participants than the comparison group. That suggests it caught people with irregular meals, such as shift workers, rather than people deliberately doing 16:8. 34 researchers signed an open letter objecting to the publicity. ([letter summary](https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/debunking-misleading-claims-the-truth-behind-the-headlines-on-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-risk/), [JAMA](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2817556))
- **The published version (2025):** It uses a different comparison group (12–14 hours) and reports a 2.35 hazard ratio. Even the authors say the link may come from other factors they couldn't fully account for, not from the short eating window. ([Medical Dialogues](https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915), [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/))
- **Another analysis of the same survey:** Under-8-hour windows were linked to more deaths mainly in people 65 and older. There was no significant link in adults under 65 once other factors were accounted for. ([Aging Cell](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12610411/))

**What the trials show**
- In a review of 99 trials, intermittent fasting worked about as well as ordinary calorie cutting for weight and heart-risk markers, with low-to-moderate certainty. ([BMJ](https://bmjgroup.com/intermittent-fasting-comparable-to-traditional-diets-for-weight-loss/))
- 16:8 eating doesn't seem to help much beyond eating less overall. It added nothing over calorie restriction alone in a 12-month trial ([NEJM](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35443107/)). It produced no metabolic benefit when calories stayed the same ([ChronoFast](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2025/12/251228020018.htm)).
- One trial found slightly more muscle loss with 16:8 ([TREAT](https://pace-cme.org/news/no-difference-in-weight-loss-or-metabolic-markers-with-time-restricted-eating/2455829)). This matters because the abstract's authors suggested muscle loss as a possible explanation.
- No trial has measured whether 16:8 changes heart attacks or deaths.

**For you:** At 45 and healthy, if 16:8 helps you keep your weight down, that benefit is real.
- Eat enough protein (about 1.2–1.6 g per kg of body weight) and do strength training to protect muscle ([trial](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnut.2024.1397090/full)).
- An earlier eating window may be a bit better than skipping breakfast, though that evidence is also observational ([NutriNet](https://hal-cnam.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-04079643), [breakfast review](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/Content/ArticleLanding/2024/FO/D3FO05705D)).
- Get your blood pressure and cholesterol checked now and then.
- If you develop heart disease, talk to your doctor before continuing.

- lxml enables free-threading only from 3.14t: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt and https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289
- The ecosystem is abandoning 3.13t. manylinux removed it on 2026-05-07 and PyTorch dropped it: https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386. Pillow 12.3 also removed its 3.13t wheels: https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/latest/releasenotes/12.3.0.html

**If you still want no-GIL later**
- 3.14 is the officially supported phase under PEP 779 (target: ≤15% single-thread overhead): https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/. Moving there requires an exception to your platform's 3.13 pin.
- Benchmark your real request mix before committing. A threaded benchmark ran slower with the GIL off (3.61 s vs 2.38 s) because of reference-count contention on shared objects: https://discuss.python.org/t/slower-performance-with-disable-gil-on-threaded-nearest-neighbor-benchmark-10m-points/95365
- NumPy's free-threading support is still experimental. Arrays are only safe to share read-only, and resizing one while another thread uses it can crash: https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/thread_safety.html
- Add a startup assertion on `sys._is_gil_enabled()`. Without it, the GIL can come back on silently and the speedup disappears: https://pycon.de/archive/2026/talks/are-we-free-threaded-ready-looking-at-where-free-threaded-python-fails/

# Why your dev container is slow on the Mac, and how to fix it

Two separate costs multiply on your Mac. Your Linux colleagues have neither.

## 1. Node runs under x86 emulation

`--platform linux/amd64` emulates the entire Node runtime (npm, bundler, dev server), not just the one x86 dependency. The official `node` image also ships for arm64 (https://hub.docker.com/_/node). Docker says emulation "can be much slower" (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/).

- **Rosetta** is the fast emulator, and it requires the Apple Virtualization framework (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/).
- **QEMU** is the fallback, and users report it is roughly 10× slower again (https://zerokspot.com/weblog/2023/11/14/rosetta-docker-desktop-feels-broken/).
- **Docker VMM** has no Rosetta support (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/).
- **Known problems:** Rosetta has pegged the CPU with Vite/Rollup and lacks AVX (https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384), and npm installs have hung on amd64 `node:20` (https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946).

## 2. `node_modules` on a bind mount

Every file access crosses from macOS into Docker's Linux VM, and `node_modules` contains tens of thousands of small files. In one measurement on the same project, `npm install` took:

| Setup | Time |
|---|---|
| Native | 4.0 s |
| Bind mount | 21.9 s |
| Bind mount + named volume for `node_modules` | 7.0 s |

Source: https://github.com/sparkfabrik/sparkdock/issues/61. VS Code recommends the same named-volume fix (https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance).

## What to do, in order

1. **Build for arm64.** Drop the platform flag and isolate the x86-only dependency, for example in a small amd64 sidecar container. This is easy if the dependency is a CLI tool and harder if it's a native Node addon. DDEV also recommends native arm64 (https://ddev.com/blog/amd64-on-apple-silicon-ddev/).
2. **Put `node_modules` in a named volume** and bind-mount only the source.
3. **If you must stay on amd64,** open Docker Desktop settings and confirm three things: Apple Virtualization framework is selected (not Docker VMM), "Use Rosetta" is on, and VirtioFS is on. Docker's docs disagree on whether Rosetta is on by default (https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/), so check rather than assume.
4. **Upgrade from Node 20.** It reached end of life on 2026-04-30.
5. **Optional:** OrbStack (https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem) or Docker's paid Synchronized File Shares (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/). Benchmark these yourself, because the vendors' speed claims are unaudited.

## Long-term risk

Apple's general Rosetta support ends with macOS 27. Built-in Intel translation for Linux VMs isn't promised beyond that (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/787530). This makes staying on amd64 a dead end.

## Confirm which cause matters most

No source measures both causes together. Run `time npm install` for each of the four combinations of {bind mount, volume} × {amd64, arm64} to see how much each contributes on your machine.

It ends with a 2x2 timing test that separates the two causes.

I recommend citing **19.11%**, or "about one in five crates." That is the share of crates on crates.io that use the `unsafe` keyword directly: **24,362 of about 127,000 crates "with significant code," measured in May 2024.** The source is the Rust Foundation's [Unsafe Rust in the Wild](https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/), computed with its [Painter](https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter) tool. The same article says **34.35%** of crates call directly into another crate that uses `unsafe`.

**Confidence:** I'm confident it's roughly 20–30%. Treat 19.11% as approximate, not exact.

Other studies with different methods land close to it:
- **2023:** 21,506 of 103,516 crates (≈20.8%), counted by text pattern matching rather than compiling ([arXiv 2308.04785](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.04785), [2412.06251](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251v2)). Both papers use the same dataset, so they count as one study.
- **Evans et al., ICSE 2020:** "less than 30%" of about 15,000 crates that still built ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752), [notes](https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/evans:icse:2020)).
- **Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020:** about 25% of 31,867 crates, according to a [secondary summary](https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/astrauskas:oopsla:2020). Another paper quotes it as [21.3%](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.02464v1). I couldn't open the original paper, so don't cite either number.

**Weaknesses an auditor may raise about the 19.11%:**
- It's a blog post, not peer-reviewed, and doesn't say how it defines "significant code" or detects `unsafe`.
- The arithmetic doesn't quite match: 24,362 ÷ 127,000 = 19.18%, so the real denominator was presumably a less-rounded figure.
- Painter only includes crates that build, so crates that fail to compile are left out.
- It's 2.5 years old. The live crates.io API reported [377,254 crates](https://crates.io/api/v1/summary) when I checked, compared with about 145,000 in May 2024.
- Popular crates use `unsafe` more often: over 50% of the most-downloaded crates, according to Evans.

**Indirect exposure is less settled.** Evans's arXiv abstract says "more than half" of crates rely on `unsafe` somewhere in their dependencies. The [ICSE page](https://2020.icse-conferences.org/details/icse-2020-papers/68/Is-Rust-Used-Safely-by-Software-Developers-) shows "more than 75%." Check which version you cite.

**Suggested wording:** "As of May 2024, about 19% of crates.io crates with significant code used `unsafe` directly (Rust Foundation), consistent with 20–30% in peer-reviewed studies from 2020–2023." Using `unsafe` doesn't mean a crate is vulnerable; the Foundation and [cargo-geiger](https://github.com/geiger-rs/cargo-geiger) both say so. For your own risk assessment, running cargo-geiger on your actual dependency tree will be more defensible than any ecosystem-wide percentage.

**Other sources read:** [Stanford, 29% of 3,638 crates](https://cs.stanford.edu/~aozdemir/blog/unsafe-rust-syntax/), [i-programmer](https://i-programmer.info/news/98-languages/17220-is-rust-safe.html), [Slashdot](https://developers.slashdot.org/story/24/05/25/2250236/rust-foundation-reports-20-of-rust-crates-use-unsafe-keyword), [Rust Foundation 2025 update](https://rustfoundation.org/?p=9784) (no newer figure), [arXiv 2602.06466](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06466v1).

**Cite this:** about **one in five crates.io crates use `unsafe` directly**. The source is the Rust Foundation, May 2024: 24,362 of about 127,000 "crates with significant code," reported as 19.11%. The same post says another **34.35%** directly call a crate that uses `unsafe`.
https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/

Present it as "≈19%, roughly 1 in 5," not "19.11%."

**Confidence:** I'm highly confident that direct use is somewhere between **19% and 29%**. Independent studies with different methods and dates all land in that range. I have little confidence in the decimals.

**Corroborating sources**
- **Evans et al., ICSE 2020.** 29% of about 15,000 crates that build use `unsafe` directly. Another 38% depend on crates that do. Among the most-downloaded crates, over 50% use it directly. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752
- **Cui et al., extended version.** 21,506 of 103,516 crates (≈20.8%) as of January 2023, found by text matching rather than compilation. Two researchers located this in §5.2.2. A third couldn't find it, so check the section before citing it. https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251
- **Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020.** Covers about 31,000 crates. Secondary sources report the share as 21.3%, 23.6% or about 25%. **Don't cite a number until it's checked against the paper** (DOI 10.1145/3428204). https://zenodo.org/records/4085004

**Weaknesses auditors will find in the headline figure**
- **It is a blog post, not peer-reviewed.** "Significant code" isn't defined.
- **The arithmetic doesn't reproduce.** 24,362 ÷ 127,000 = 19.18%, not 19.11%. Against all ~145,000 crates it would be about 16.8%.
- **The tool only counts some crates.** The Painter tool includes only crates that build, using default features and the latest version of each. https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter
- **The data is from 2024.** No registry-wide re-count from 2025–26 was found.

**What matters for supply-chain risk**

Direct use understates exposure. If you count dependencies, more than half of crates reach `unsafe` code:
- Evans found over 50% of crates rely on `unsafe` once dependencies are included.
- The Foundation's 19% + 34% ≈ 53% counts only direct calls, so the full transitive share is likely higher.

**Short answer: no. WAL mode on a shared NFS mount does not work. Switching to rollback mode could make it run, but it still wouldn't be safe enough for production.**

**Why WAL breaks across hosts**
- SQLite's documentation says plainly: "All processes using a database must be on the same host… WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL coordinates through a memory-mapped `-shm` index, and separate machines cannot share memory. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- NFS doesn't keep memory-mapped files in sync between clients. Red Hat closed the related bug as WONTFIX, noting that NFS servers don't track which clients have a file mapped. https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=179911
- This has happened in practice. OpenAI's Codex documentation says Linux hosts sharing an NFS home can corrupt a WAL-mode SQLite database, so Codex switches to rollback mode on NFS. https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/network-file-systems

**Why rollback mode is still risky**
- Rollback mode depends on file locks working correctly over NFS. SQLite's FAQ says to avoid putting the database on NFS when multiple processes may access it at the same time. https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html, https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- SQLite isn't tested over a network, and failures are rare and hard to reproduce, so passing your own tests proves little. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- During a network blip, NFSv4 locks can expire. Current kernels then return I/O errors to the application. Older kernels, or the `recover_lost_locks` setting, can let two servers write at the same time. https://access.redhat.com/solutions/1179643
- Performance: every transaction locks the whole database and takes several network round trips. SQLite says to use a client/server database when several servers write to the same data. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

**What I'd do instead**
1. **Use PostgreSQL.** It's the simplest choice for three servers and 20 writes per second, and it's SQLite's own first suggestion. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
2. **Or keep SQLite on one host's local disk** with WAL mode, and have the other two servers send reads and writes through a small service on that host. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
3. **Or use replicated SQLite:**
   - rqlite (https://rqlite.io/docs/faq/) or dqlite (https://github.com/canonical/dqlite) replicate with Raft.
   - LiteFS has one writer and replicates asynchronously, so a failover can lose the most recent writes. https://docs.fly.io/litefs/how-it-works

If you go ahead with NFS anyway, use rollback (DELETE) mode. First, test that a lock taken on one host actually blocks the other hosts, and run that test under failure conditions too. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-09-08-detect-unsafe-nfs-smb-embedded-database-locking/markdown

**Other sources consulted:** https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html, https://www.sqlite.org/atomiccommit.html, https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html, https://nfs.sourceforge.net/, https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/, https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg56864.html, https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=629296

# No. WAL mode on a shared NFS mount across three servers will not work reliably.

All three researchers came to the same conclusion, and it rests mainly on SQLite's own documentation.

## Why

**1. WAL cannot work across hosts.** WAL coordinates readers and writers through a shared-memory index (the `-shm` file, accessed via mmap). Processes on different machines cannot share memory. SQLite's docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." The `-shm` file is never fsynced and uses the host's byte order, so it was never meant to be shared between machines.
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/walformat.html

**2. NFS itself is a corruption risk, even without WAL.** SQLite's docs say network use is untested and "at the user's risk." They also say locks "have been known to operate incorrectly… This has led to database corruption," and they name NFS specifically.
- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html

On the NFS side, Linux guarantees cache consistency only at file open and close, and it gives no mmap coherence between clients.
- https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html

NFSv4 locks are held on a lease, and the server can revoke them if a client loses contact.
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7530

**3. Passing tests prove little.** In one report, two Grafana servers shared SQLite on NFS without problems for two weeks, and then the database became corrupted. SQLite maintainers warn that NFS can claim a lock or a commit succeeded when it didn't, and the damage may only show up later.
- https://community.grafana.com/t/two-grafana-servers-with-single-sqlite3-databse-on-nfs/2734
- https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/02c1a784a2830a3d?raw

**Counter-evidence:** one forum user runs SQLite on NFSv4 with up to 12 hosts and reports "very few" problems. This is probably rollback mode, not WAL, and they say it limits scaling. Nobody has published measured failure rates.
- https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/341635c1ff

## What to do instead

At 20 writes per second, either of these is simple:

1. **Use Postgres or MySQL.** This is the standard fix, and SQLite's own docs recommend it for multi-server writes.
   - https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
2. **Keep SQLite on one server's local disk**, with WAL enabled, and have the other two servers send reads and writes to it through an API. One host can easily handle 20 writes per second.

**Avoid this option:** rollback-journal mode on NFS. SQLite lists it as allowed (many readers or one writer, never both at once), but every write would need a lock round-trip over the network. You would also still depend on your NFS server's locking being correct, so you'd need cross-host fault testing and reliable backups. Never use the `nolock` or `local_lock` mount options for this, because each client then sees only its own locks.

# 28 April 2025 Iberian blackout: established causes and open disputes

**Caveat:** I couldn't extract text from the official report PDFs, so technical details below come from ENTSO‑E's web pages, official press notes, and trade-press summaries of the reports. Check the details against the [final report PDF](https://eepublicdownloads.blob.core.windows.net/public-cdn-container/clean-documents/Publications/2025/iberian-blackout/Final%20Report%20on%20the%20Grid%20Incident%20in%20Spain%20and%20Portugal%20on%2028%20April%202025.pdf) before the brief goes out.

## Established by official investigations

- **ENTSO‑E expert panel, final report (20 Mar 2026)** [1]: no single cause. The factors were oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive-power control, differing voltage-regulation practices, rapid output cuts and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven stabilisation capabilities. Together they caused fast voltage rises and a cascade of generator trips. It was the first blackout of this kind in Continental Europe.
- **Sequence, from the factual report (3 Oct 2025)** [2][3]:
  - A 0.63 Hz oscillation (12:03–12:08) and a 0.21 Hz inter-area oscillation (12:19–12:22) were damped, but the damping measures raised Iberian voltage.
  - Trips began at 12:32:57 and exceeded 2.5 GW by 12:33:18, with voltage above 435 kV.
  - Iberia lost synchronism with Europe at 12:33:19. Load shedding could not stop a collapse driven by overvoltage.
- **Deficiencies the final report found** [3][4][5]:
  - Several synchronous units hit their reactive-power reference less than 75% of the time.
  - Shunt reactors were switched by hand.
  - Under Spanish rules, renewables ran at a fixed power factor.
  - Spain's 400 kV band allowed up to 435 kV, leaving little margin before protection trips.
  - At least 10 disconnections didn't meet requirements.
  - The voltage-control rule (PO 7.4) set no dynamic-performance requirements for conventional generators.
- **Spanish government committee (Jun 2025)** [6]: the cause was multifactorial. Voltage-control resources were either not scheduled in sufficient amount, or did not deliver what was scheduled, or both. Some disconnections appeared improper.
- **Cyberattack ruled out:** the Audiencia Nacional (Spain's national court) provisionally closed its case in January 2026, relying on reports from INCIBE and CCN, Spain's national cybersecurity agencies [6].

## Contested or unresolved

- **Who is responsible:** ENTSO‑E says assigning blame is outside its remit [7].
  - REE (the Spanish TSO) says it committed no breach and that its scheduling is not among the causes [7].
  - Utilities (Aelec, Endesa) blame poor scheduling of synchronous generation by REE [8][9].
  - In April 2026, CNMC (the Spanish regulator) opened sanction proceedings, including a "very serious" case against REE. It stressed this does not attribute the cause to anyone [10]. I found no outcome as of November 2026 [11].
- **Unexplained:**
  - Why generators missed their reactive-power setpoints [7].
  - Why about 500 MW of output fell at the start, and what caused most of the overvoltage trips [5].
  - Data gaps include unmonitored PV below 1 MW [3].
- **Source of the oscillation:** REE named a PV plant in Badajoz [12]. ENTSO‑E points to converter-driven instability in southern Spain [3]. Iberdrola is suing REE over being blamed [13].

## Sources

2. https://www.modernpowersystems.com/analysis/six-months-after-the-iberian-blackout-new-expert-panel-report-reveals-the-what-but-not-the-why/

# Short answer: there's no good reason to stop because of this headline

**Where the "91%" comes from.** It was an unreviewed 2024 conference poster. The researchers used NHANES survey data on about 20,000 US adults and compared people whose eating window was under 8 hours with people eating over 12–16 hours. The short-window group had a cardiovascular-death hazard ratio of 1.91. There was no link with death from all causes. The AHA's own release says the finding doesn't show that time-restricted eating *caused* the deaths. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death?print=1

The peer-reviewed version (2025) reported a higher HR of 2.35. It still found no all-cause effect, and the authors list residual confounding as a possible explanation. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/

**Why the evidence is weak**
- **Eating window measurement.** It came from just two 24-hour food recalls. Nobody was asked whether they fasted deliberately or did so for years. A short recorded window can simply mean incomplete records, shift work, poverty, or illness. https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/
- **Group size and imbalance.** The under-8h group was small, roughly 2% of the sample. It reportedly had about 60% more smokers. More than 30 researchers called the conclusions overstated, though many of them work on time-restricted eating. https://nutritioninsight.com/news/scientists-dispute-study-linking-time-restricted-eating-to-poor-heart-health.html
- **The supporting study has the same flaw.** A second NHANES analysis found a U-shaped pattern, with the lowest risk at 11–12 hours. Its excess risk was concentrated in adults over 65, but it used the same two-recall method. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12610411/
- **Your routine may not match the risk group.** An exact 16:8 schedule sits at the boundary, and it is unclear whether it would even count as "under 8 hours."

**What the trials show.** Randomized trials find no harm to blood pressure, cholesterol or glucose. They also find little benefit beyond ordinary calorie control:
- Over 12 months, adding time-restricted eating to calorie restriction gave no extra weight loss. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35443107/
- One 16:8 trial found a small loss of lean mass. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32986097/

No trial has lasted long enough to measure deaths.

**What I'd do**
- If 16:8 is working for you, you're healthy, and you eat a good diet, continuing is reasonable.
- If the headline still worries you, widening your window to 10–12 hours costs you little, since the trials suggest the window itself adds little.
- Keep your protein up and do some strength training, given the lean-mass finding.
- Have a routine check of blood pressure and lipids.

## Short answer: this study alone isn't a reason to stop

**What the study actually found**
- The "91%" came from a March 2024 American Heart Association conference abstract. Researchers looked at about 20,000 people in a US national survey (NHANES). The 8-hour figure applied to people who ate within **less than** 8 hours a day, so your exact 16:8 wasn't the group tested. ([AHA](https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death?print=1))
- That group was only 414 people, and 31 of them died of heart disease. It had more smokers, a higher BMI, and three to four times more Black participants than the rest. ([TCTMD](https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality), [letter from 34 researchers](https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/debunking-misleading-claims-the-truth-behind-the-headlines-on-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-risk/))
- Eating windows came from just **two days** of self-reported food intake, then were assumed to hold for 8 or more years. The surveys ran from 2003 to 2018, so many of these people were probably shift workers or poor rather than deliberate fasters. Some short windows may simply be meals people forgot to report. ([Science Media Centre](https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/))
- The peer-reviewed 2025 version reported a hazard ratio of 2.35 (roughly 2.35 times the risk), but with a wide uncertainty range (1.39–3.98). It found no link with death from all causes, and the authors themselves say leftover confounding may explain it. ([Abstract](https://www.lifescience.net/publications/1424832/association-of-eating-duration-less-than-8-h-with-/))
- A separate NHANES analysis also found higher risk below 8 hours, but it has the same two-day weakness. ([Aging Cell](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12610411/))

**What the trials show**
- Randomized trials, mostly lasting 3 to 12 months, show small improvements in weight and blood pressure. No trial has measured heart attacks or deaths. ([BMJ](https://bmjgroup.com/intermittent-fasting-comparable-to-traditional-diets-for-weight-loss/), [Frontiers](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full))
- A one-year trial found 8-hour eating no better than plain calorie cutting. ([NEJM summary](https://pace-cme.org/2022/05/09/time-restricted-diet-is-not-more-beneficial-than-calorie-restriction-alone))
- Two real downsides showed up: some **loss of muscle** ([NEJM Journal Watch](https://clinician.nejm.org/fasting-shows-no-weight-loss-benefit-standard-meals-randomized-trial-nejm-jw.FW117079), [BMJ Medicine summary](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20260122/When-you-eat-matters-early-time-restricted-eating-improves-metabolic-health.aspx)), and higher LDL cholesterol with windows **shorter than** 8 hours.

**Rough sense of scale.** My own estimate: a healthy 45-year-old's chance of dying from heart disease over 8 years is around 1% or less. Even if the doubling were real, the added risk is under about 1 percentage point. ([CDC](https://cdc.gov/nchs/blog/posts/2021/11/19.html))

**Bottom line.** The evidence is weak (low quality, one small group, likely confounded). Experts disagree on what to do: some say keep going if it's working ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853)), others suggest a pause. If you continue, these steps address the real downsides:
- Don't shrink the window below 8 hours.
- Eat enough protein and do strength training to protect muscle.
- Focus on what you eat, not only when.
- Check your LDL and blood pressure at your next physical.
- An earlier window (for example 9:00–17:00) may be slightly better than a late one.

A 10–12 hour window is a reasonable fallback if you'd rather hedge. No guideline currently tells healthy people to stop.

**No, you shouldn't run this on 3.13t.** It was always labelled experimental, the tools for building packages for it have dropped it, and lxml never supported free-threading on it. If you need parallel threads for CPU-bound work, the real option is 3.14t, which means changing your platform's version pin.

**Why 3.13t is ruled out**
- Python's own docs call 3.13t experimental and expect bugs. Single-threaded code runs about 40% slower on it. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- 3.14 is the first officially supported free-threaded build (PEP 779). Its single-threaded penalty is about 5–10%. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ · https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html
- The standard Linux build images removed 3.13t on 2026-05-07, so projects can no longer build packages for it. PyTorch and Pillow have dropped it. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386 · https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/pull/2787 · https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/latest/releasenotes/12.3.0.html
- The latest NumPy (2.5.4) and pydantic-core (2.50.4) list only 3.14t free-threaded packages in the parts of their PyPI pages I could read. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/ · https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/
- Regular bug-fix releases for 3.13 ended in October 2026. https://peps.python.org/pep-0719/

**Your dependencies on 3.14t**
- **NumPy:** works. NumPy lists free-threaded Python as Tier 2, and 2.5 improved how well ufuncs scale across threads. Arrays aren't locked, so give each thread its own arrays or only read shared ones. https://numpy.org/neps/nep-0057-numpy-platform-support.html · https://numpy.org/doc/2.5/release/2.5.0-notes.html · https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/thread_safety.html
- **pydantic:** support is officially "experimental", and pydantic warned its own tests were still flaky. https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-11-release
- **lxml: the blocker.** As of lxml 6.0.2, the stable 3.14t packages turn the GIL back on when lxml is imported. If you force it off, it will likely crash under threads. Real support exists only in the 7.0 alphas (latest a3, June 2026). https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289 · https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/ · https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a3/
- An extension that turns the GIL back on does it for the whole process. https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/

**What to do**

# Is free-threaded 3.13t production-ready for your service?

**No, not for this stack.** Do not ship on 3.13t. Plan the free-threaded move around a platform upgrade to 3.14t, and use a process pool on regular 3.13 until then.

## Why 3.13t is out

- **CPython itself calls 3.13t experimental.** The docs warn of bugs and a single-thread slowdown of about 40%, because the specializing interpreter is off. Some objects are never freed, so memory use grows. Importing a C extension that isn't marked thread-safe silently turns the GIL back on. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- **The ecosystem is dropping 3.13t.**
  - cibuildwheel deprecated cp313t in April 2026. https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/pull/2787
  - manylinux removed 3.13t on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch followed. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- **Your three dependencies have no current cp313t wheels.** The latest NumPy, pydantic-core and lxml releases appear to ship only cp314t and cp315t wheels. The researchers saw truncated file lists, so this is likely but not fully confirmed. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files · https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files · https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
- **lxml is the hard blocker.**
  - Stable 6.x re-enables the GIL on import. Forcing it off has caused segfaults. https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289
  - Real free-threading support starts in 7.0 (pre-release, labelled experimental, 3.14t and later only). Whether 7.0 final is out yet is unclear. https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/

## Why 3.14t is the target

- PEP 779 made free-threading officially supported starting with 3.14. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/
- Single-thread overhead drops to roughly 5–10%. https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html
- One benchmark showed a 3.09× speedup with 4 threads on 3.14t, versus 2.2× on 3.13t. https://simonwillison.net/2025/Oct/8/python-314-is-here-how-fast-is-it/

## What to do

1. **Now:** stay on GIL 3.13. Use multiprocessing for CPU parallelism.
2. **Ask for the platform pin to move to 3.14.** Then trial 3.14t in staging:
   - Check that `sys._is_gil_enabled()` returns `False` after all imports.

3. **Benchmark your real workload** on 3.14t against multiprocessing on regular 3.14, measuring both throughput and memory. Two separate costs multiply on your Mac. Your colleagues pay neither: Linux reads host files directly, and their laptops are presumably x86, so nothing is emulated.

**1. `node_modules` on a bind mount (the main cost for npm install)**
On macOS, containers run inside a Linux VM, so every file operation on a bind mount crosses the VM boundary. npm install writes tens of thousands of small files, which is the worst case. In a controlled 2025 test, npm install took 3.37 s natively, 9.53 s with the whole project bind-mounted (VirtioFS), and 3.61 s with `node_modules` in a named volume. https://www.paolomainardi.com/posts/docker-performance-macos-2025/ Docker itself recommends keeping dependency trees out of bind mounts. https://www.docker.com/blog/file-sharing-with-docker-desktop/

**2. `--platform linux/amd64` emulates everything**
Node, npm and every native module run as x86 code, not just the one dependency. With Rosetta, this is slower than native. Without it, Docker falls back to QEMU, which "can be much slower than native" (one user saw about 10x). https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/ · https://zerokspot.com/weblog/2023/11/14/rosetta-docker-desktop-feels-broken/ Rosetta works only with the Apple Virtualization engine, not Docker VMM. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/ Docker's docs disagree on whether Rosetta is on by default, so check your settings. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/

**What to do, in order**
1. Put `node_modules` and any cache/build folders in a named volume, and run `npm install` inside the container.
2. In Docker Desktop settings, confirm the engine is **Apple Virtualization framework**, **Rosetta** is on, and file sharing is **VirtioFS**. `docker info` shows the active setup.
3. Best long-term fix: build the main image as native arm64, and run only the x86-only dependency in its own amd64 service or stage. DDEV recommends this approach. https://ddev.com/blog/amd64-with-rosetta-on-macos/ Check whether that binary needs AVX, which Rosetta doesn't support. https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
4. If it's still slow, try synchronized file shares (may require a paid plan) or OrbStack. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/ · https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem

**To confirm the split**, time npm install four ways: arm64 vs amd64, each with and without the bind mount. No published benchmark separates the two costs for your exact setup.

**1. The whole Node toolchain runs as emulated x86.** Because of `--platform linux/amd64`, every `node` and `npm` process on your M3 is translated from x86. Rosetta is "nearly on par with native" by Docker's own claim ([4.25](https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/)). If you're on QEMU instead, it's 5–20x slower ([oneuptime](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-16-docker-mac-apple-silicon/view), [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/), [zerokspot](https://zerokspot.com/weblog/2023/11/14/rosetta-docker-desktop-feels-broken/)). You fall back to QEMU if Rosetta is off, or if you chose the Docker VMM engine, which doesn't support Rosetta ([VMM](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/), [settings](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/)). Also, Apple limits Rosetta to some old games starting with macOS 28, which comes after the one you're on now ([Apple](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102527)). Whether x86 Linux containers keep working is unconfirmed ([apple/container#76](https://github.com/apple/container/issues/76)).

**2. `node_modules` sits on a bind mount.** Every file access has to cross from the Linux VM to macOS, and `node_modules` is tens of thousands of small files ([OrbStack](https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem), [techearl](https://techearl.com/docker-bind-mounts-slow-mac-windows)). Reported penalties are about 3.5x for installs ([eastondev](https://eastondev.com/blog/en/posts/dev/20251217-docker-mount-comparison/)), and 3.7x more on top of that if you're still on gRPC FUSE instead of VirtioFS ([Geerling](https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2022/new-docker-mac-virtiofs-file-sync-4x-faster/)).

**What to do, in order:**
1. **Check settings now.** Engine (VMM) = Apple Virtualization framework, file sharing = VirtioFS, and "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation" turned on.
2. **Put `node_modules` in a named volume** mounted over the bind mount (`node_modules:/app/node_modules`). VS Code ([docs](https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance)) and GOV.UK ([ADR](https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/repos/govuk-docker/adr/0003-use-docker-volumes-for-improved-macos-performance.html)) both recommend this. The downside is that your Mac editor can't see those files. Installs made inside the container also get Linux-native binaries.
3. **Stop running everything as amd64.** Use native `node:20` (arm64) and keep only the x86 dependency under emulation, for example in a separate amd64 service container. It may also be possible to run that one x86 binary inside an arm64 container through Rosetta, but I haven't confirmed that, so test it first. This fix gives the biggest gain and keeps working if Rosetta goes away.
4. **Fallbacks:** Docker's Synchronized file shares (paid plans, 2–10x faster per Docker; [docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/)), cloning the repo into a container volume, or OrbStack.
5. **If hot reload misses changes,** turn on polling (`CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING` or Vite's `usePolling`). It costs extra CPU ([Vite](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-watch)).

Other sources: [Docker VirtioFS](https://www.docker.com/blog/speed-boost-achievement-unlocked-on-docker-desktop-4-6-for-mac/), [Docker perf](https://www.docker.com/blog/what-are-the-latest-docker-desktop-enterprise-grade-performance-optimizations/), [dkechag](https://dev.to/dkechag/improving-docker-file-performance-on-macos-537k), [CNCF](https://www.cncf.io/blog/2023/02/02/docker-on-macos-is-slow-and-how-to-fix-it/), [Lima](https://lima-vm.io/docs/config/multi-arch), [DDEV](https://docs.ddev.com/en/stable/users/install/performance/), [Compose watch](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/file-watch/).

**No, this isn't safe.** Your plan uses WAL, which simply doesn't work across hosts. Even without WAL, SQLite's developers advise against having several machines share a database over NFS.

**Why WAL fails here**
- WAL coordinates connections through shared memory (the `-shm` file, which SQLite memory-maps). SQLite's docs say "all processes using a database must be on the same host… WAL does not work over a network filesystem." https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- Richard Hipp, SQLite's author, says WAL will "malfunction" when clients are on different hosts. If a test seemed to work, the test wasn't thorough enough. https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html
- NFS doesn't keep memory-mapped files in sync between clients. https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=179911
- OpenAI's Codex docs say multiple hosts opening the same WAL database over NFS can corrupt it. Codex switches to DELETE (rollback) mode to avoid this. https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems

**Rollback mode is still risky**
- SQLite says locking on network filesystems is often buggy, and that a lock failure can let two hosts write at once and corrupt the file. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html, https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html, https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html, https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html, https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- On NFSv4, a client can lose its locks if its lease expires, for example during a network blip. Writes then fail with EIO, and turning lock recovery back on "may cause data corruption." https://access.redhat.com/solutions/1179643
- The corruption can stay hidden and show up later. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/02c1a784a2830a3d?raw
- Grafana users who shared a SQLite file over NFS reported corruption after two weeks. https://community.grafana.com/t/two-grafana-servers-with-single-sqlite3-databse-on-nfs/2734
- GoToSocial doesn't support SQLite on NFS at all. https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/
- One long-running user did fine over NFS, but only because their server honored locks and syncs exactly, and they still had some problems. https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg111568.html

**What to do instead** (20 writes/sec is easy for any of these)
1. **PostgreSQL.** This is the best fit for three app servers writing to one database. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
2. **One server owns the SQLite file** on its local disk, in WAL mode, and the other two send reads and writes to it through an internal API. This is SQLite's own recommended "proxy" setup. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
3. **Replicated SQLite**, where all writes go through one leader node:
   - rqlite: https://rqlite.io/docs/faq/
   - dqlite: https://canonical.com/dqlite/docs/explanation/replication
   - LiteFS: https://docs.fly.io/litefs/how-it-works

If you keep any SQLite on NFS, first test whether a lock taken on one host really blocks the others, across server restarts and network drops. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-09-08-detect-unsafe-nfs-smb-embedded-database-locking/view

I read 27 sources in total. Fetches of a Plex forum thread, a Stack Overflow mirror and a kernel patch page were blocked, so I didn't rely on them.

- SQLite's WAL page says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL coordinates writers through a memory-mapped `-shm` file, and separate machines cannot share that memory. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

**Why rollback mode is still risky**
- SQLite's corruption guide names "network filesystems and NFS in particular" as having locking bugs that corrupt databases. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- The FAQ says fcntl() locking "is broken on many NFS implementations." https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html
- The Linux NFS client does not keep data fully consistent across clients without application-level serialization. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html
- NFSv4 locks can be revoked when a lease expires, so after a network partition two hosts could both write. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7530.html

- Every lock also costs a network round-trip, which adds latency at 20 writes/s. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/c04bf5be0e

1. **Use PostgreSQL or MySQL.** This is the simplest choice for three app servers.
2. **Keep SQLite in WAL mode on local disk on one host,** and have the other two servers reach it through a small API or proxy on that host.
3. **Rollback mode on NFS** is offered only as damage limitation, "at your (and your customers') peril."

**Caveat:** none of the sources measured actual corruption rates for rollback mode on modern Linux NFSv4. The evidence is official warnings plus anecdotes. Even so, every source agrees, so I would choose option 1 or 2.

# Unsafe code on crates.io: recommended figure and confidence

**Cite: about 19% of crates.io crates used `unsafe` directly as of May 2024** (Rust Foundation: 24,362 crates, 19.11%). An independent 2023 scan using a different method found about 21%, which supports it.

**Confidence:** Moderate that the true share in 2023–24 was about 19–21%. Low on the decimal place. The figure is also about 2.5 years old, and the registry has since grown to about 200,000 crates.

## Sources

1. **Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (21 May 2024).** Of about 145,000 crates, about 127,000 "contain significant code". Of these, 24,362 use `unsafe`, given as 19.11%. A separate 34.35% directly call into a crate that uses `unsafe`. https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
   Auditors may flag these points:
   - 24,362 ÷ 127,000 = 19.18%, so the denominator was rounded.
   - The post says "of all crates", but 19.11% only works against the ~127,000 crates with significant code, not the ~145,000 total.
   - "Significant code" is never defined.
   - The Painter tool only counts the latest version of each crate, only crates that build, and only default features.
   - No data snapshot has been published, so the figure can't be reproduced. https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter
2. **Cui et al., 2023 (preprint, not peer-reviewed).** 21,506 of 103,516 crates (about 20.8%) as of January 2023. The scan searched source text and included yanked crates. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04785
3. **Evans et al., ICSE 2020.** The abstract says "less than 30%" of libraries use `unsafe` directly, and more than half can't be fully checked by the compiler once dependencies are counted. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752

## For supply-chain risk

The direct share understates exposure. Pair it with the dependency figures:
- 34.35% of crates call directly into unsafe-using crates (Rust Foundation). This is a lower bound.
- More than half are affected once dependencies count (Evans).

## Present older numbers carefully

Older estimates (about 29%, 2016–2020) used different methods. Don't present the fall from 29% to 19% as a trend.

## Don't cite

- **23.6% / 76.4% (Astrauskas, OOPSLA 2020):** no researcher could check these against the original paper.

# Don't put a shared SQLite database on NFS

**Decision:** No. Don't let three servers open one SQLite file over NFS. Use PostgreSQL or MySQL. If you want to keep SQLite, run it on local disk on one host and have the other two servers reach it through a small service or API.

**Rests on:** WAL mode cannot work across machines.

- **The design rules it out.** WAL coordinates writers through a memory-mapped `-shm` file, and separate hosts cannot share memory. SQLite's docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem" (https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html).
- **SQLite's author agrees.** D. Richard Hipp said that if WAL seems to work over NFS, "you didn't test it enough" (https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html).
- **Others have hit it in practice.**
  - Firefox saw WAL fail on NFS (https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=629296).
  - OpenAI's Codex docs report corruption from WAL on shared NFS (https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems).
  - Two Grafana servers sharing one file ran fine for two weeks, then corrupted it (https://community.grafana.com/t/two-grafana-servers-with-single-sqlite3-databse-on-nfs/2734).

This follows from how SQLite works, so it applies to your setup without needing a test.

**Switching to rollback-journal mode doesn't rescue the plan.**

- SQLite calls network use "at your (and your customers') peril," says it is untested there, and names NFS as the classic case of broken locking (https://sqlite.org/useovernet.html, https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html, https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html).
- NFS client caching gives no freshness guarantee while a file is open (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html).
- NFSv4 lock leases can be revoked after a stall or a network partition (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7530.html).
- When locking fails, the corruption is silent and shows up late.
- Each write would also take a whole-database lock with network round-trips, which is a poor fit for 20 writes per second (https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/c04bf5be0e).

**Not verified:** Nobody has measured how reliable rollback mode is on a modern Linux NFSv4 setup like yours. That would only matter if you insisted on sharing the file, and it still wouldn't make that a supported setup.

**Next check:** None needed. If you go the single-host route, put the SQLite file on that host's local disk, not on the NFS mount.

The official investigations agree that this was an **overvoltage collapse with several causes, not a cyberattack and not a single fault**. Who is responsible is still disputed and has not been settled legally.

**Established by official investigations**
- **Spanish government committee (17 June 2025):** The system lacked enough dynamic voltage control. Some plants scheduled for voltage control did not regulate as the rules require, and some disconnections were improper. It also criticised Red Eléctrica (REE) for rescheduling rather than replacing a thermal plant that withdrew the evening before. It found no evidence of a cyberattack. [1]
- **Criminal court (12 January 2026):** The Audiencia Nacional provisionally closed its criminal case, finding no sign of sabotage. [2]
- **ENTSO-E expert panel, final report (20 March 2026):** It found no single point of failure. [3][4][5]
  - Two oscillations came first: a 0.63 Hz converter-driven forced oscillation and a 0.2 Hz inter-area one. The steps that damped them pushed voltage up.
  - Voltage control was ineffective. Renewables ran at a fixed power factor, several synchronous units did not reach their reactive-power targets, and shunt reactors were switched by hand.
  - The 400 kV limit of up to 435 kV left little margin before trips. Overvoltage trips cascaded, some at settings that did not comply with the rules.
  - The rules did not require dynamic voltage control and set no penalties.
  - The panel assigns no legal responsibility.
- **Spanish regulator CNMC:** It calls the event multifactorial and says tools to prevent it existed at the time. In April 2026 it opened a "very serious" case against REE and "serious" cases against generators, while stating these do not attribute the cause. [6][7][8]
- **Portuguese regulator ERSE (May 2026):** The origin was in Spain, and the Portuguese operator REN ran restoration correctly. [9]

**Contested (mark as such in the brief)**
- **Responsibility:** REE says no cause is attributable to it. [10] Endesa and Iberdrola blame REE's scheduling and slow reaction. [11] Endesa also claims a conflict of interest because REE sat on the panel. [12] REE questions the CNMC's impartiality. [13] I found no final CNMC decision.
- **Source of the oscillation:** REE's chair says it was a solar plant in Badajoz. Iberdrola denies its Núñez de Balboa plant was the source. [14][15]
- **Data gaps:** Missing records mean the cause of some disconnections was never found. [5]
